clue.text: Gilbert's graduate at Castle Adamant

parts.note: Castle Adamant is Princess Ida's women's university in Gilbert and Sullivan's opera, and one of its girl graduates is named in the libretto

explanation.surface: A question about a minor character in a comic opera.
explanation.walkthrough: Princess Ida (Gilbert and Sullivan) is set at Castle Adamant, a university for women; Chloe is one of its girl graduates.
explanation.definitionFit: Chloe is the name of a girl graduate in the women's college of Gilbert's Princess Ida.

clue.text: Carved hen clumsily — finished with St Leger's fish

indicators.note: something done clumsily is botched, so the letters of carved hen are jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone hacks badly at a carved hen and then turns to fish.
explanation.walkthrough: The old name for the chub appears in St Leger's writing; 'clumsily' shuffles CARVEDHEN.
explanation.definitionFit: An old English dialect name for the chub, a freshwater fish.

clue.text: Extreme reached by Kipling, before renewal

definitions.meaning: an extreme is the furthest point anything may go
Kipling's 1932 story collection is titled ... and Renewals, so the word comes just before the renewal part of the title

explanation.surface: Kipling hits the furthest point before a fresh start.
explanation.definitionFit: A boundary or utmost point is an extreme; Kipling's collection Limits and Renewals supplies the literary sense.

clue.text: Strangely drole fuss in prosperous area described by Raleigh

indicators.note: done strangely means in an odd arrangement, so the letters of drole are reordered

parts.note: fuss means ado, as in much ado about nothing

explanation.surface: An odd, comic commotion takes place in a wealthy region Raleigh wrote about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strangely' reworks DROLE, and the fuss word follows. Sir Walter Raleigh's Discovery of Guiana tells of the search for the golden city.
explanation.definitionFit: The legendary city of gold sought in South America, a byword for a place of great wealth.

clue.text: Sign of trademark diagram

parts.note: a company's trademark emblem is its logo
a graph is a diagram plotting values

explanation.surface: A trademark drawing is a kind of sign.
explanation.definitionFit: A written character standing for a whole word, such as an ampersand, is a sign of this sort.

clue.text: Said to be flower of euphuism

definitions.text: Said to be flower of euphuism

indicators.note: said means spoken, so the word for the flower is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: a lily is a flower

explanation.surface: Someone reputed to be the finest bloom of an ornate prose style.
explanation.walkthrough: John Lyly's Euphues gave its name to euphuism, the ornate Elizabethan prose style; he is its 'flower', and his name sounds like the bloom.
explanation.definitionFit: The Elizabethan author whose romance Euphues started the euphuistic style was its finest flowering.

clue.text: Exemplary work of Heller

definitions.meaning: exemplary means behaving perfectly, like a well-behaved child
Joseph Heller's 1979 novel bears this idiom as its title

explanation.surface: A fine piece by the author of Catch-22.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for a perfectly behaved child also titles a Joseph Heller novel.

clue.text: Willa Cather seems to have written of this general's skill at cards

definitions.text: Willa Cather seems to have written of this general's skill at cards

parts.words: Willa Cather seems to have written of this general's skill at cards
parts.note: Read playfully, bridge is a card game, so the title seems to praise a famous general's card play

explanation.surface: A novelist apparently wrote about an ancient commander's card skills.
explanation.walkthrough: Cather's novel Alexander's Bridge is about an engineer, but the title read as a card game suggests Alexander the Great playing bridge.
explanation.definitionFit: The Macedonian general known as the Great is the commander named in Cather's novel title.

clue.text: Comfort offered as the strange start of title

indicators.note: strange means odd, so the letters of as the are rearranged

explanation.surface: Consolation is offered in an odd opening to a book name.
explanation.walkthrough: Comfort is the writer Alex Comfort, whose collection Haste to the Wedding begins with the answer, so 'Comfort offered' points to his title rather than meaning solace.
explanation.definitionFit: Alex Comfort's poetry collection Haste to the Wedding opens with this word.

clue.text: Buffoon at Navarre court is sick inside, in Boyd's book

indicators.note: inside says the word for sick goes within the name of the buffoon

parts.note: Don Armado is the boastful Spaniard at the King of Navarre's court in Love's Labour's Lost
sick means ill

explanation.surface: A court jester in Navarre is unwell in William Boyd's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Love's Labour's Lost is set at the court of Navarre, where Don Armado is the comic braggart.
explanation.definitionFit: William Boyd's 1998 novel is titled Armadillo.

clue.text: Robert and Wilfred, for example

parts.note: Robert the social reformer and Wilfred the war poet share a surname, so they are two people of that name

explanation.surface: Two men's first names given as a pair of examples.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Owen founded New Lanark; Wilfred Owen wrote war poetry.
explanation.definitionFit: The reformer Robert and the poet Wilfred share the same surname, so together they make a plural of it.

clue.text: Tree in drama — to be taken as a whole

indicators.note: drama suggests theatrical upheaval, so the letters of tree in are rearranged

explanation.surface: An actor-manager appears in a play as the complete production.
explanation.walkthrough: Herbert Beerbohm Tree was a celebrated actor-manager, so 'Tree in drama' reads as theatre; 'drama' rearranges TREEIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Something whole and complete, considered with nothing left out, is entire.

clue.text: Anthologist's friend has serious following

definitions.note: the 's stands for is, so the definition is the anthologist himself

indicators.note: following says the word for serious comes after the word for friend

parts.note: a pal is a friend
grave means serious

explanation.surface: An anthology editor's companion is of solemn character.
explanation.walkthrough: Francis Turner Palgrave compiled The Golden Treasury, the Victorian poetry anthology.
explanation.definitionFit: Francis Turner Palgrave edited The Golden Treasury of English verse.

clue.text: Land at Bourget to reach international city

definitions.meaning: Paul Bourget's 1892 novel is set in a cosmopolitan Rome and bears this title
a city whose people come from many nations

explanation.surface: Touching down at Le Bourget airport to get to a global city.
explanation.walkthrough: Le Bourget is a Paris airport, which makes 'Land' look like a flight verb; here it means the world of Paul Bourget's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: A city inhabited by people of many nations is a world city; also the title of Bourget's novel.

clue.text: Novelist suggests daughter eager to stay (5, )

parts.note: avid means eager
to lodge is to stay somewhere

explanation.surface: A writer hints that his daughter is keen to remain.
explanation.definitionFit: The English author of campus novels such as Changing Places and Nice Work.

clue.text: Anonymous work of 6/257

parts.note: an unsigned love card sent in February, and also the title of an 1832 novel by the writer at 6 and 25

explanation.surface: A piece without author credit by a named writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 6/25 is George Sand, whose novel bears this title; the 7 looks like a stray from the printed page.
explanation.definitionFit: A card sent unsigned on 14 February, and also George Sand's early novel.

clue.text: Prepare for publication in printed item

indicators.note: in says the answer sits inside the letters of the words that follow

explanation.surface: Getting a printed item ready to go out.
explanation.definitionFit: To get a text ready for printing by correcting and revising it.

clue.text: Hairy-chested bedfellow of Waugh's undergraduate

parts.note: Sebastian Flyte in Brideshead Revisited carries a furry companion named Aloysius around Oxford

explanation.surface: A rugged roommate of a student in a Waugh novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hairy-chested' suggests a macho man; it is literally furry. Sebastian's Aloysius in Brideshead Revisited is the toy.
explanation.definitionFit: Aloysius, Sebastian Flyte's furry toy companion, is a stuffed bear.

clue.text: Pollock's Toy Theatre's high-end price

parts.note: toy theatre sheets were sold penny plain or at a higher price coloured, and Pollock's shop kept the tradition

explanation.surface: The top cost of an item in a London toy theatre shop.
explanation.walkthrough: Victorian toy theatre sheets were 'penny plain, twopence coloured'; Pollock's is a famous London toy theatre maker and shop.
explanation.definitionFit: The coloured sheets cost two old pennies, double the plain ones.

clue.text: Part of misleading lore

indicators.note: misleading means leading astray, so the letters of lore are led out of order

explanation.surface: A section of deceptive folklore.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor's part in a play is the character played.

clue.text: 14's location for bumping into old friends, perhaps

definitions.text: 14's location for bumping into old friends, perhaps

parts.words: 14's location for bumping into old friends, perhaps
parts.note: the novelist at 14 set a campus novel among academics who keep meeting at conferences, and people say this phrase on unexpected meetings

explanation.surface: A place where a novelist runs into old acquaintances.
explanation.walkthrough: 14 is David Lodge, whose novel of that title follows academics meeting around the globe; the phrase is what people exclaim on a chance meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation on a chance encounter, and the title of David Lodge's 1984 novel.

clue.text: Part of simple Yellow Pages entry for piano manufacturer

indicators.note: Part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A listing in a business directory for a piano maker.
explanation.definitionFit: Pleyel is a French firm of piano makers, so it would be listed in a trade directory.

clue.text: Writer to run away from faithful wife

parts.note: a pen is a writing instrument
to elope is to run away to marry

explanation.surface: An author flees from a loyal spouse.
explanation.definitionFit: Odysseus's wife in Homer, who waited twenty years for his return.

clue.text: Language is up, but below average

indicators.note: in a down clue, below says this piece sits under the word for average

parts.note: par is the average or normal level

indicators.note: up in a down clue means the word is is read from bottom to top

explanation.surface: A tongue is rising, though it is substandard.
explanation.definitionFit: The Persian dialect of the Zoroastrian community of India is a language name.

clue.text: Like Gladys Mitchell's merciful exit

parts.note: Gladys Mitchell's first detective novel is titled with a quick end, the kind of passing thought merciful

explanation.surface: Describing a kind death in a crime writer's story.
explanation.walkthrough: Gladys Mitchell's 1929 debut novel is Speedy Death; a merciful death is a quick one.
explanation.definitionFit: A quick death is merciful, and Gladys Mitchell's first Mrs Bradley mystery is named for one.

clue.text: The Remains of the Day after Whitsun

definitions.meaning: the glowing remains of a fire, from the title The Remains of the Day
the ... Days are fasting days, including the Wednesday, Friday and Saturday after Whitsun

explanation.surface: Ishiguro's novel title split into its parts.
explanation.walkthrough: The Remains of the Day is Kazuo Ishiguro's novel; Ember Days are church fast days in each season, one set following Whit Sunday.
explanation.definitionFit: A glowing piece left in a dying fire, and one of the church's quarterly fast days.

clue.text: Poor weather reported by Bromfield

definitions.meaning: wet, showery conditions are poor weather
Louis Bromfield's novel The Rains Came reports a monsoon season in India

explanation.surface: Bad weather described by an American novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Wet weather with showers, as in the monsoon of Bromfield's The Rains Came.

clue.text: "When the lesson comes … I suppose it will come in some — shape" (Kingsley, Two Years Ago)

definitions.text: "When the lesson comes … I suppose it will come in some — shape" (Kingsley, Two Years Ago)

parts.words: "When the lesson comes … I suppose it will come in some — shape" (Kingsley, Two Years Ago)
parts.note: a quotation from Charles Kingsley's novel with one word missing, describing a form in which a lesson could be taken in

explanation.surface: A line from a Victorian novel about a lesson to be learnt.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gap from Charles Kingsley's 1857 novel Two Years Ago.
explanation.definitionFit: Something capable of being learnt; the quoted lesson will come in a form one can grasp.

clue.text: Idle aside wrongly quoted, yet highly regarded

indicators.note: wrongly means incorrectly, so the letters of idle aside are given in the wrong order

explanation.surface: An offhand remark is misquoted, yet the speaker is admired.
explanation.definitionFit: To be thought of as perfect is to be regarded very highly.

clue.text: Mistake appearing in Elizabeth comedy

definitions.meaning: a mistake is a slip or blunder
Shakespeare's Elizabethan play The Comedy of ... has the word in its title

explanation.surface: A blunder turns up in an Elizabethan play.
explanation.definitionFit: A blunder, and the word in the title of Shakespeare's Comedy of Errors.
